_comment: Mutation survivors accepted as a baseline for the binding sweep (the membership walk, the context it carries, and the frontend). The nightly ratchet fails when a survivor appears outside this set, and when an entry is no longer a survivor. Regenerate with `python scripts/mutation_gate.py --baseline walk --update` after a sweep, and only ever let this set shrink. Entries are the survivor line without its line:col position, so they survive unrelated code motion.

_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/build/classes.rs:: The guard `!origin.is_instance_of::<PyType>()` keeps a class origin from asking the `typing_extensions` table, and the mutant asks it for a class and skips it for a form. On the interpreter this sweep runs, 3.12 with `typing_extensions` installed from the lock, that module's `Required` and `NotRequired` are `typing`'s own objects, from 3.11 on, and the loop above has already matched them: the table answers `false` for every origin that reaches the guard, on either side of it, and the mutant moves cost alone. So the frontend's arms for that module's own objects answer what the `typing` arms already answered, and a mutant of them moves nothing a test can read. They answer where the module defines objects of its own -- 3.10, or the stand-in `a_typing_extensions_form_reads_as_its_typing_spelling` installs on an interpreter that cannot import the module, which is where that corpus row kills this mutant. The arm dies with the 3.10 floor.

`says.is_none() && !origin.is_instance_of::<PyType>()` becomes `says.is_none() || ...`, which asks the `typing_extensions` table where `typing`'s own marker has already answered, and for a class origin where nothing has. The table answers as the guard's skip does in both: a class is none of its forms, and on the interpreter this sweep runs, 3.12 with `typing_extensions` installed from the lock, that module's `Required` and `NotRequired` are `typing`'s own objects, from 3.11 on, so the table matches the marker the loop above matched and gives the answer it gave, where a module defining objects of its own matches none of `typing`'s. The guard is the walk's cost alone, the reading of the table skipped where the answer is known, and a mutant of it moves nothing a test can read; its sibling `delete ! in qualified_required #1` is accepted for the same reason.

So the arms for that module's own objects answer what the `typing` arms already answered, and a mutant of them moves nothing a test can read. They answer where the module defines objects of its own -- 3.10, or the stand-in `a_typing_extensions_form_reads_as_its_typing_spelling` installs on an interpreter that cannot import the module, which is where that corpus row kills this mutant. The two arms die with the 3.10 floor.

_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/index.rs: d: `if !fields.is_empty()` read as `if fields.is_empty()`: an attribute record with no fields gains a plan of no names, and one with fields gains none, so each attribute is looked up through a name made per call rather than the one the index interned. The lookup is by name equality, so it finds the same attribute: the verdict and the report hold, and only a `__getattribute__` that tests a name's identity rather than its text could tell. The cost is the instruction gate's, which reads the mutant at 288% more on `--binding-object-walk`'s fifty-field dataclass and refuses it. The arms of `collect` beside it are not equivalent: a record left without its plan is read by its entries, which moves a report, and `a_union_of_records_reports_alike_wherever_it_sits` kills them.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/index.rs: r: The traversal `__traverse__` hands the cycle collector. Every object it yields is an interned `str`, and a `str` refers to nothing, so it is no edge of a cycle and a collector that never sees one collects the same. The method exists because a traversal omitting an owned reference is wrong on its own terms: `gc.get_referents` on a validator sees the omission, the one reading of a traversal a program can make, and it moves nothing the library promises, so no test is written for it.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/memo.rs: re: `<=` differs from `<` only at a reference naming index 128, the first past the plan's `u128`. `plan` names nothing for a table longer than `PLANNED_DEFINITIONS`, and a validator's references name its own definitions, so no reference the plan reads names that index. The comparison keeps an index outside the table from shifting a `u128` past its width, a panic in a debug build and a wrapped bit in a release one, for a schema no validator holds.

The arming, `bits | USED | ARMED`, read as `bits | USED ^ ARMED`: `^` binds tighter than `|`, so the mutant is `bits | (USED ^ ARMED)`, and on two distinct bits `^` is `|`. The word set is the same word.

The restore, `bits & !ARMED | outer`: `outer` is the armed flag the member was walked inside, or nothing, and the mask has just cleared that flag, so `^` sets it where `|` does and leaves it clear where `|` does. The word after the member is the same word.

`calling`, the definitions whose own bodies call code, folds one bit per definition, `1 << at` at the definition's own index, and the enumeration reaches each index once: no bit is folded in twice, and on bits folded in once `^` sets what `|` sets. The set is the same, and so is every bit of the plan read from it.

`remembered`, the definitions reaching no code the walk calls, folds one bit per definition, `1 << at` at the definition's own index, and the enumeration reaches each index once: no bit is folded in twice, and on bits folded in once `^` sets what `|` sets. The set is the same, and so is every bit of the plan read from it.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/record: Cannot change an answer. A mapping of a `str` key and an `int` value falls to the arm every other pair of scalar kinds takes, which asks the same two tests through `scalar_admits` and reads the dict through the same scan; only the dispatch on each half's kind at every entry is added. That is cost, and the instruction gate counts it: `scripts/perf_gate.py --binding-mapping`, a `dict[str, int]`, reads 17.5% more without the arm, past its 2% ceiling.

`plan.by_name.len() == fields.len()` holds of every plan, which lists each field once, so `||` takes the plan for every record: a record whose clause reads keys and declares no more than `SMALL_OBJECT` fields among them. The plan and the search answer alike for such a record -- each reads the document's last value for every field and asks the clause of the keys left -- and report alike; besides the cost what moves is the order the fields are read in, and with it whether a predicate on an earlier field runs before a later one refuses, which no page promises for a parsed document, and the instruction gate's `--binding-json-open` reads it: that shape's record declares one field. `a_record_reading_keys_takes_its_plan_past_a_small_object` holds the crossing itself.

The counter it disables lets a closed record holding exactly its own keys skip a scan that would find nothing: stuck at zero, the count matches only an empty value, so every other record falls through to the scan, and the scan reports what the count would have. A value a predicate rewrites at the same size while it is explained is the one place the two differ -- the scan reports the key swapped in, which the skip would not -- and a report about a value moved mid-explanation is the best effort the move allows, which `tests/test_mutation.py` states. For a value that holds still only the cost moves, and `--binding-explain` reads it at 6%. The other half of the same condition is not equivalent and is killed by tests/test_mutation.py: a value that grows while it is explained leaves the count matching entries it no longer has, which is why the length is read again before the skip is taken.
_accepted.crates/valgebra-py/src/check/walk/scalar: The mutant's body is the function's own: the error is a parameter, and a parameter is dropped where its function returns, so `()` drops it at the very place `drop(err)` does -- inside `set_aside`, out of line, which is the whole of what the function is for. Inlined into `check_refine`'s loop over its constraints, the drop's read of whether the thread is attached has its thread-local address taken ahead of the loop, once for every refined value; out of line, it is taken only where the error a string holding a lone surrogate raises is dropped. Compiled, the two differ by one jump on the cold path -- the original inlines `PyErr`'s drop, the mutant calls it -- and `check_refine` is the same in both, so the drop stays out of line either way and neither a test nor a count can tell them apart.
